concepts.title: Root Mean Square Values of AC
concepts.definition: Mains ratings quote the root-mean-square value, the steady value that would heat a resistor identically; it equals the peak of the sine wave divided by root two, so a 220 V line actually swings to about 311 V.
concepts.key_idea: RMS exists because heating goes as the square of current, which never averages to zero even though the signed current does.
concepts.textbook_ref: leph107.txt section 7.2 (Eqs. 7.6-7.9, 220 V line with 311 V peak, Exercise 7.2)
question_patterns: the peak voltage of a supply is 300 V; what is the rms voltage
an rms current of 10 A flows; what peak current does the sine reach
convert between peak and rms values of an ac signal
why do meters read the rms value rather than the average of an ac wave
how many volts is the peak of a 220 V household line
compute 0.707 times the amplitude for the given alternating quantity

solution_steps.explain: the conversion constant is sqrt(2), about 1.414
the effective value is the amplitude over sqrt(2)

concepts.title: Resistance and Power from RMS Ratings
concepts.definition: With rms values the dc toolkit transfers unchanged: a bulb rated P watts on a V volt line has resistance V squared over P, and the mean heating over a cycle reads I squared R or simply P over V for the current.
concepts.key_idea: Average ac power equals rms current times rms voltage because the oscillating half of the sine squared averages away.
concepts.textbook_ref: leph107.txt section 7.2 (Eqs. 7.4-7.7, Example 7.1 100 W bulb on 220 V, Exercise 7.1)
question_patterns: a bulb is rated 100 W at 220 V; find its resistance and the rms current through it
compute the resistance of a heater from its power rating and the line voltage
what average power does a resistor dissipate when an rms current flows
find the net energy-per-second delivered over a full ac cycle
why is the average power nonzero while the average current is zero
a 100 ohm resistor sits on a 220 V 50 Hz supply; find the rms current and cycle power

solution_steps.explain: resistance follows from P = V squared over R
R equals V squared over P for a resistive device
the rms current is the rating over the line voltage

concepts.title: Phasor Picture of AC Circuits
concepts.definition: A phasor is an arrow spinning at the source's angular speed whose vertical projection reproduces the sinusoidal voltage or current at each instant; its length is the peak value and the angle between two phasors is their phase gap.
concepts.key_idea: Resistor phasors point the same way (in phase); inductor current trails by a quarter turn, capacitor current leads by a quarter turn.
concepts.textbook_ref: leph107.txt section 7.3 (Fig. 7.4, phasors as rotating vectors)
question_patterns: what does the projection of a phasor on the vertical axis represent
why can voltage and current phasors point in different directions
explain how a rotating arrow generates a sine graph
what does the angle between two phasors tell you
are phasor quantities true vectors
sketch the phasors for a resistor circuit and read off the phase difference

solution_steps.explain: each phasor rotates counter-clockwise at omega with length equal to the amplitude
the vertical shadow at time t equals amplitude times sin(omega t)
the angle between phasors is the lead or lag of one oscillation relative to the other

concepts.title: Inductive Reactance
concepts.definition: An inductor chokes a changing current in proportion to omega L, a resistance-like quantity in ohms; the current amplitude is the voltage over this reactance and the current peaks a quarter cycle after the voltage.
concepts.key_idea: Reactance grows with frequency, and the net energy flow over a cycle is zero - the inductor only borrows and returns it.
concepts.textbook_ref: leph107.txt section 7.4 (Eqs. 7.12-7.14, Example 7.2 25 mH at 50 Hz, Example 7.5 iron rod)
question_patterns: a 25 mH inductor sits on a 220 V 50 Hz supply; find the reactance and rms current
compute XL equal to 2 pi nu L for the given inductor
why does the current in a pure inductor lag the voltage by a quarter cycle
what happens to a bulb in series with a coil when an iron core slides in
how does inductive reactance change when the supply frequency rises
find the average power consumed by a pure inductor over a cycle

solution_steps.explain: omega is 2 pi times the line frequency
XL equals omega times the inductance
the rms current is voltage over reactance, lagging by pi over 2

concepts.title: Capacitive Reactance
concepts.definition: A capacitor passes alternating charge through repeated charge-discharge with an opposition of 1 over omega C ohms; current amplitude is voltage over this reactance and the current peaks a quarter cycle before the voltage.
concepts.key_idea: Reactance shrinks as frequency or capacitance grows - the opposite trend of an inductor - and a capacitor dissipates nothing per cycle.
concepts.textbook_ref: leph107.txt section 7.5 (Eqs. 7.16-7.19, Example 7.3 lamp and capacitor, Example 7.4 15 microF)
question_patterns: a 15 microF capacitor joins a 220 V 50 Hz line; find the reactance and the rms and peak currents
compute 1 over 2 pi nu C for the given capacitor
what happens to the reactance and current if the frequency doubles
why does a lamp glow with ac but not dc when a capacitor is in series
why does capacitor current lead the applied voltage
how much power does a pure capacitor take over a full cycle

solution_steps.explain: omega equals 2 pi times the frequency
XC is 1 over omega C
the rms current is voltage over reactance, leading by pi over 2

concepts.title: Impedance of a Series LCR Circuit
concepts.definition: Element voltages in a series loop add as phasors, not plain numbers, so the loop's total opposition is Z equal to the square root of R squared plus the squared gap between capacitive and inductive reactance.
concepts.key_idea: Because VR and the LC combination stand at right angles, element voltages can exceed the source voltage individually while the phasor sum still matches it.
concepts.textbook_ref: leph107.txt section 7.6.1 (Eqs. 7.25-7.26, Example 7.6 RC circuit paradox)
question_patterns: find the impedance of a series combination of resistor, inductor and capacitor
compute Z from R, XL and XC for the given element values
why can the resistor and capacitor voltages add to more than the supply voltage
a 200 ohm resistor and 15 microF capacitor run on 220 V 50 Hz; find the current
how do you combine element voltages that are a quarter cycle apart
what replaces simple resistance when a loop mixes R, L and C

solution_steps.explain: omega equals 2 pi times the supply frequency
XL equals omega L
XC equals 1 over omega C
the L and C voltages fight each other, leaving XC minus XL
Z is the hypotenuse over R and the reactance gap
the rms current is the supply voltage over Z

concepts.title: Phase Angle and Lead or Lag
concepts.definition: The tilt between source voltage and current obeys tan phi equal to XC minus XL over R: positive phi means a capacitive circuit with current leading, negative means inductive with current lagging, and phi zero means pure resistance.
concepts.formula: phase sign follows the sign of react_c minus react_l
concepts.key_idea: The sign of phi settles which way the current tips relative to the voltage, and the phasor method describes the steady state only.
concepts.textbook_ref: leph107.txt section 7.6.1 (Eq. 7.27, capacitive vs inductive dominance, Example 7.8 part b)
question_patterns: find the sign of the phase angle for given XL and XC values
does the current lead or lag the source voltage in this loop
compute tan phi from the reactances and resistance
when is a series circuit called predominantly capacitive
what phase angle do you get for R equal 3, XL equal 8, XC equal 4
why does a negative phase angle mean an inductive circuit

solution_steps.explain: subtract XL from XC to see which opposition dominates
tan phi equals the reactance gap over the resistance
positive phi: current leads (capacitive); negative: current lags (inductive); zero: resistive

concepts.title: Resonant Frequency of an LCR Circuit
concepts.definition: Sweeping the supply frequency makes XL and XC cross where omega nought equals 1 over root LC; there the reactances cancel, the impedance collapses to R and the current peaks - the trick behind radio tuning.
concepts.key_idea: Resonance needs both L and C so their voltages can cancel; at the peak the current is vm over R and only R dissipates.
concepts.textbook_ref: leph107.txt section 7.6.2 (Eq. 7.28, Example 7.9 resonance at 35.4 Hz, Example 7.10 metal detector, Exercises 7.6-7.8)
question_patterns: find the angular frequency of free oscillations for a charged capacitor joined to an inductor
compute the resonant frequency from L and C values
what is the impedance and current at resonance for the given circuit
why can a circuit with only L or only C never resonate
how does radio tuning exploit the resonance peak
a 30 microF capacitor and 27 mH inductor oscillate freely; find omega nought

solution_steps.explain: resonance depends only on the product of inductance and capacitance
omega nought is 1 over its square root
the ordinary frequency is omega nought over 2 pi

concepts.title: Average Power and the Power Factor
concepts.definition: Mean ac power is the product of rms voltage, rms current and cos phi, where phi is the voltage-current phase gap; pure L or C runs at cos phi zero, drawing wattless current that delivers no energy.
concepts.key_idea: Only the resistor burns energy; a low power factor forces extra current for the same delivered power, so transmission lines waste I squared R - capacitors are added to lift cos phi.
concepts.textbook_ref: leph107.txt section 7.7 (Eqs. 7.29-7.30, cases i-iv, Example 7.7 transmission loss)
question_patterns: find the average power drawn by a circuit from its rms values and power factor
why is the current in a purely inductive circuit called wattless
compute VI cos phi for the given circuit data
how does a poor power factor raise transmission losses
what is the power dissipated at resonance in a series LCR loop
which circuit element alone dissipates energy in an ac loop

solution_steps.explain: the apparent power is rms voltage times rms current
multiplying by cos phi leaves the real, dissipated power

concepts.title: Transformer Turns Ratio
concepts.definition: Mutual induction across a shared core ties the two windings: voltages scale with turns while currents scale inversely, so stepping the voltage up always steps the current down by the same factor.
concepts.key_idea: An ideal transformer conserves power - Vs Is equals Vp Ip - which is exactly why high-voltage transmission keeps line currents small.
concepts.textbook_ref: leph107.txt section 7.8 (Eqs. 7.33-7.36, 220 V 10 A to 440 V 5 A example)
question_patterns: a transformer has 100 primary and 200 secondary turns with 220 V 10 A input; find the output
compute the secondary voltage from the turns ratio
what is a step-up transformer and what happens to its current
find the secondary current when the voltage is stepped down
why does stepping up the voltage not violate energy conservation
determine whether the given winding counts step the voltage up or down

solution_steps.explain: the ratio is secondary turns over primary turns
voltages follow the turns ratio directly
the ideal power balance divides the current by the same ratio

concepts.title: Losses in a Real Transformer
concepts.definition: Practical transformers leak flux between windings, waste heat in winding wire, churn eddy currents in the iron core, and pay a hysteresis bill for repeatedly re-magnetising it; laminated cores, thick wire and interleaved windings fight these losses.
concepts.key_idea: A well-built core still returns over 95 percent of the input power, but each named loss has its own hardware remedy.
concepts.textbook_ref: leph107.txt section 7.8 (loss list i-iv, transmission and distribution discussion)
question_patterns: list the ways a real transformer wastes energy
why is a transformer core laminated
how does flux leakage reduce the secondary output and how is it reduced
why is thick wire used for low-voltage high-current windings
what is hysteresis loss and which material choice limits it
explain why stepping up voltage does not create free energy

solution_steps.explain: stray flux that misses the secondary carries no output power; interleaving the coils confines it
winding resistance burns I squared R, so heavy current windings use thick wire
laminations cut eddy-current heating and low-hysteresis steel cuts reversal loss
